title: Beyond Fixed Biases: Decoding the Role of Reasoning Uncertainty in MLLM Modality Conflicts
claim: Controlling difficulty independently per modality lets us measure each one's uncertainty and relate relative uncertainty to which modality wins a conflict.
layout: 3 panels: left tall input panel, right top and bottom; dashed borders
description: Three dashed-border panels. Panel (a), on the left, shows the question 'What color is the square?'. A vision input labeled Color = Red appears as three images of increasing clutter, dv = 0, 1, 2. A textual input labeled Color = Blue appears as three statements of increasing indirection, dt = 0, 1, 2. Panel (b), top right, feeds an image plus the question and a text plus the question into an MLLM box, with arrows to two entropy histograms labeled Hv (red) and Ht (blue). Panel (c), bottom right, shows a conflict input combining the red-square image, the word Blue and the question. Next to it is the formula ΔHrel = 2(Ht − Hv)/(Ht + Hv). Below the formula, a blue-to-red gradient arrow runs from Text-easier and Text-prefer to Vision-easier and Vision-prefer. Red and blue color-code the modalities throughout.
caption: Overview of the analytical framework. (a) We create inputs with independently controllable visual (dv) and textual (dt) difficulty. (b) We measure the model’s perceived uncertainty for each modality via output entropy (Hv, Ht). (c) We then use the relative uncertainty (∆Hrel) to analyze the model’s choice when faced with a conflict.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) must resolve conflicts when modalities provide contradictory information, a behavior we term "modality following". We propose a framework that decomposes this behavior into case-specific relative preference uncertainty and stable inherent preference. Across diverse MLLMs and benchmarks, the probability of following a modality consistently decreases as its relative preference uncertainty increases, a trend robust to alternative uncertainty indices. This regularity defines a "balance point'' where modality preferences are evenly matched, offering a capability-disentangled measure of modality bias. Layer-wise probing further shows that ambiguous cases near the balance point trigger middle-to-late-layer "concept oscillations," where top predictions vacillate between modality-supported answers. Finally, we demonstrate the framework's utility for preference steering through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We find that data efficiency is governed by preference uncertainty: training on easy samples (where one modality dominates) fails to generalize, whereas targeting the identified ``boundary cases" is essential for robust preference alignment and suppressing internal vacillation.
